attacks.name: Phishing
attacks.overview: Social engineering through email, messaging or voice calls to trick a person into revealing credentials, approving access or running malicious content.
methodology: Research targets and pretexts (roles, suppliers, internal tools)
Deliver a lure: email link or attachment, SMS, or a phone call impersonating IT
Harvest credentials or MFA codes, or get the user to run a payload
Use the access for mailbox takeover, internal tools or further compromise

incident.title: Twitter account takeover via phone spear-phishing

facts.text: NYDFS found that the hackers accessed Twitter's systems by calling Twitter employees and claiming to be from Twitter's IT department.
The hackers posted "double your bitcoin" messages from compromised accounts and stole over $118,000 worth of bitcoin from consumers.

incident.analysis: The attack bypassed technical email filtering entirely, which shows why voice phishing must be part of awareness training and help-desk verification procedures.

indicators: Look-alike or newly registered sender domains
Sign-ins from new devices or locations shortly after a reported lure
Inbox rules created to hide or forward mail
Users reporting unexpected IT calls or MFA prompts
logSources: Proxy / DNS logs for clicks on lure domains
detections: Correlate a delivered phishing email with a sign-in from a new IP for the same user within hours
Alert on creation of inbox rules that move, delete or forward messages
Flag impossible-travel or anomalous-token sign-ins after password reset
controls: Phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2)
DMARC/SPF/DKIM enforcement and external-sender banners
Verified call-back procedure for IT and help-desk requests
Easy one-click reporting and regular simulation training
response: Identify all recipients and remove the message from mailboxes
Reset credentials and revoke sessions/tokens for users who interacted
Review mailbox rules, OAuth consents and recent sign-ins
Block lure domains and sender infrastructure
Notify and brief affected users

attacks.name: Ransomware
attacks.overview: Malware that encrypts data and systems to extort payment, now commonly combined with data theft and threats to leak it.
methodology: Gain initial access (stolen credentials, exposed RDP/VPN, phishing, exploited vulnerabilities)
Escalate privileges and move laterally to domain controllers and file servers
Exfiltrate data for double extortion
Disable defences and delete backups / shadow copies
Deploy encryption widely, often via GPO or remote execution tools

incident.title: Colonial Pipeline ransomware attack

facts.text: On 7 May 2021 a ransomware attack on Colonial Pipeline led to long queues at gas stations across the U.S. eastern seaboard and panic buying of fuel.

CISA describes the incident as the moment the vulnerability of a highly connected society became a nationwide issue. In the following two years it created stopransomware.gov and launched the Joint Ransomware Task Force with the FBI.

incident.analysis: The public impact came from fuel-supply disruption rather than data loss, which shows how ransomware against one company's IT can cascade into critical-infrastructure effects.

indicators: Shadow-copy deletion (vssadmin, wmic shadowcopy)
Mass file renames with new extensions
Security tools stopped or tampered with
Large outbound transfers before encryption
detections: Alert on vssadmin/wbadmin/bcdedit commands that delete or disable recovery
High-rate file modification by a single process (canary files)
New services or scheduled tasks created on many hosts in a short window
controls: Offline, immutable and regularly tested backups
MFA on all remote access and privileged accounts
Network segmentation, especially between IT and OT
Least privilege and tiered administration
Rapid patching of internet-facing systems
response: Isolate affected hosts and segments; do not power off before capturing volatile evidence where feasible
Disable compromised accounts and reset privileged credentials (including KRBTGT twice)
Determine the initial access vector and scope of data theft
Restore from known-good backups after eradication
Engage legal, regulators and law enforcement as required

attacks.name: SQL injection
attacks.overview: Injecting SQL syntax into application input so that the database runs attacker-controlled queries. Attackers can then read or change data, or run commands on the server.
methodology: Find input reaching the database (parameters, headers, cookies)
Probe with syntax-breaking characters and boolean/time-based payloads
Extract schema and data (UNION, error-based or blind techniques)
Escalate: write files, create accounts or execute commands where the DBMS allows

incident.title: MOVEit Transfer mass exploitation (CVE-2023-34362)

facts.text: The CL0P group exploited a previously unknown SQL injection vulnerability in MOVEit Transfer, beginning on 27 May 2023.
Exploitation led to installation of the LEMURLOOT web shell, which was used to steal data from MOVEit Transfer databases.

incident.analysis: SQL injection remains impactful in commercial products, not just custom code; vendor software exposed to the internet needs the same scrutiny as in-house applications.

indicators: Quotes, comments (--, /* */), UNION SELECT, SLEEP() or WAITFOR in request parameters
Spikes of HTTP 500 errors from one client
Unusual database queries or large result sets
New script files in web directories
detections: WAF/IDS signatures for SQLi patterns (tune for false positives)
Many 500 responses for a single parameter from one IP
Database account executing statements outside its normal pattern
controls: Parameterised queries / prepared statements everywhere
Least-privilege database accounts per application
Input validation and output encoding
WAF as a compensating control, not the primary fix
Timely vendor patching
response: Block the source and, if confirmed, take the vulnerable endpoint offline or patch
Review database and web logs to scope data accessed
Hunt for web shells and new accounts
Rotate database and application secrets
Assess notification obligations for exposed data

attacks.name: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
attacks.overview: Injecting script into pages that other users view, so it runs in the victim's browser with the site's privileges. Attackers use this to hijack sessions, deface pages or spread worms.
methodology: Find input that is reflected or stored and later rendered without encoding
Craft a payload that runs in the page context
Deliver it: stored on the site, or reflected via a crafted link
Act as the victim: steal tokens, perform actions or spread

incident.title: The Samy worm on MySpace

facts.text: A stored XSS payload placed on a MySpace profile caused visitors to add the author as a friend and copy the payload to their own profiles.
The worm spread to over one million users in under 20 hours.

incident.analysis: Self-propagating XSS shows that client-side injection can have platform-wide impact; modern defences such as CSP and HttpOnly cookies limit, but do not replace, correct output encoding.

indicators: <script>, event handlers (onerror=, onload=) or javascript: in parameters
Unexpected outbound requests from pages to unknown domains
CSP violation reports
Sudden spread of identical content across user profiles
logSources: Application logs of stored user content
detections: WAF rules for XSS payload patterns
Monitor CSP violation reports for injected script sources
Alert on stored content containing script or event-handler syntax
controls: Context-aware output encoding
Strict Content Security Policy (no inline script)
Safe DOM APIs (textContent) instead of innerHTML with data
HttpOnly and SameSite cookies
Template frameworks with auto-escaping
response: Remove stored payloads and fix the vulnerable rendering path
Invalidate sessions that may have been stolen
Review CSP reports and logs to scope affected users
Deploy or tighten CSP

references.title: Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet

attacks.name: Brute-force attacks
attacks.overview: Repeatedly guessing passwords for one or more accounts, often using default or common credentials against exposed services such as SSH, RDP, Telnet or web logins.
methodology: Find exposed authentication services
Try password lists, default credentials or credential-stuffing pairs
Use successful logins for access, persistence or to recruit devices into botnets

incident.title: Mirai botnet built from default IoT credentials

facts.text: Mirai malware scanned for Internet of Things devices and infected them by logging in with a built-in list of common default usernames and passwords.
The resulting botnets were used for large distributed denial-of-service attacks.

incident.analysis: Credential guessing at internet scale succeeds wherever default credentials ship unchanged; the fix lies with device configuration and vendor defaults rather than detection.

indicators: Many failed logons from one source (4625, sshd 'Failed password')
Failures across sequential usernames such as admin, root or test
Success immediately after a run of failures
Account lockouts (4740)
detections: Threshold: more than N failures from one IP in M minutes (tune per service)
Failure-then-success sequence for the same account and source
Authentication attempts from known-bad or anonymising infrastructure
controls: Disable default credentials; enforce unique strong passwords
MFA on all remote access
Remove direct internet exposure of RDP/SSH/Telnet
Rate limiting, lockout or progressive delays
Fail2ban-style automated blocking
response: Block offending sources
Check for any successful logon and investigate that session
Reset affected credentials
Reduce exposure of the targeted service

references.title: Heightened DDoS Threat Posed by Mirai and Other Botnets (TA16-288A)

attacks.name: Password spraying
attacks.overview: Trying a few common passwords against many accounts, staying under per-account lockout thresholds.
methodology: Enumerate valid usernames (email format, directory leaks)
Try one or two likely passwords across all accounts, slowly
Rotate source IPs to avoid rate limits
Use any successful account for further access

incident.title: Midnight Blizzard password spray against Microsoft

facts.text: Microsoft reported that Midnight Blizzard used a password spray to compromise a legacy, non-production test tenant account.
The actor then used that account's permissions to access a small percentage of Microsoft corporate email accounts, including senior leadership.

incident.analysis: Forgotten non-production accounts without MFA are a recurring weak point; account inventory matters as much as password policy.

indicators: One source failing against many distinct accounts
Same password-failure pattern across accounts in a short window
Sign-in attempts against disabled or non-existent accounts
Legacy-protocol authentication attempts
detections: Count distinct usernames with failures per source IP per hour
Low-and-slow detection across distributed IPs using the same user-agent
Alert on success from a source that also produced many failures
controls: MFA on all accounts including test and service accounts
Block legacy authentication protocols
Banned-password lists
Smart lockout and IP reputation-based blocking
Remove stale and unused accounts
response: Identify any successful sign-ins from spraying sources
Reset and revoke sessions for affected accounts
Review permissions granted to compromised accounts (including OAuth apps)
Block source infrastructure

references.title: Microsoft Actions Following Attack by Nation State Actor Midnight Blizzard

attacks.name: Privilege escalation
attacks.overview: Gaining higher permissions than initially obtained, for example SYSTEM or domain administrator, through vulnerabilities, misconfigurations or stolen credentials.
methodology: Enumerate local and domain privileges, services and patch levels
Exploit a vulnerable service or driver, or abuse misconfigured permissions
Obtain SYSTEM/root or administrative tokens
Use elevated access to dump credentials or disable defences

incident.title: PrintNightmare (CVE-2021-34527) emergency directive

facts.text: CISA reported active exploitation, by multiple threat actors, of CVE-2021-34527 in the Windows Print Spooler service, which allows a remote authenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code with SYSTEM privileges.
Federal civilian agencies were directed to stop and disable the Print Spooler service on all Active Directory domain controllers and to apply the July 2021 cumulative updates.

incident.analysis: Services running as SYSTEM on domain controllers are high-value escalation paths; disabling unneeded services shrinks attack surface regardless of patch status.

indicators: Special privileges assigned to new logons (4672) for unexpected accounts
New members added to privileged groups (4728/4732/4756)
Driver or DLL loads from unusual paths by system services
Processes running as SYSTEM spawned by user applications
detections: Alert on additions to Domain Admins / Enterprise Admins
User-context process spawning a SYSTEM child process
Spooler service loading DLLs from non-standard directories
controls: Prompt patching (prioritise KEV)
Disable unnecessary services, especially on domain controllers
Least privilege and LAPS for local admin passwords
Tiered administration model
response: Contain affected hosts
Review privileged group changes and revert unauthorised ones
Reset credentials of exposed privileged accounts
Patch or mitigate the exploited flaw across the estate

references.title: Emergency Directive 21-04: Mitigate Windows Print Spooler Service Vulnerability

attacks.name: Lateral movement
attacks.overview: Moving from an initially compromised host to other systems using stolen credentials, remote services or exploits, until the attacker reaches high-value assets.
methodology: Discover hosts, shares and trust relationships
Harvest credentials from the foothold
Authenticate to other hosts with RDP, SMB/PsExec, WMI or WinRM, or exploit network services
Repeat until reaching domain controllers or data stores

incident.title: NotPetya (Petya) destructive malware

facts.text: The malware spread laterally using the EternalBlue SMB exploit (MS17-010) as well as harvested credentials with legitimate tools such as PsExec and WMI.
It encrypted the master boot record and files, rendering systems unusable.

incident.analysis: Combining an exploit with credential-based movement meant fully patched hosts were still infected when admin credentials were reused; patching and credential hygiene are both required.

indicators: Logons of type 3/10 between workstations
PsExec service installation (7045, PSEXESVC)
WMI process creation on remote hosts
One account authenticating to many hosts in minutes
detections: Workstation-to-workstation SMB/RDP/WinRM connections
New service creation by a remote logon
Graph analytics: an account fanning out to an abnormal number of hosts
controls: Block SMB/RDP between workstations with host firewalls
Unique local admin passwords (LAPS)
Patch SMB vulnerabilities; disable SMBv1
Privileged access workstations and tiering
response: Map the movement path from authentication logs
Isolate affected hosts and disable used accounts
Reset credentials that were exposed on compromised hosts
Apply segmentation rules to stop further spread

attacks.name: Credential dumping
attacks.overview: Extracting password hashes, plaintext credentials or Kerberos material from memory (LSASS), the SAM or the Active Directory database (NTDS.dit).
methodology: Obtain local admin or SYSTEM privileges
Read LSASS memory, or copy SAM/SYSTEM hives
On domain controllers, copy NTDS.dit via shadow copies or ntdsutil
Crack or pass the hashes to authenticate elsewhere

incident.title: Volt Typhoon NTDS.dit extraction

facts.text: The joint advisory described Volt Typhoon extracting the Active Directory database (NTDS.dit) from domain controllers, including by creating Volume Shadow Copies.
The actor used built-in Windows tools such as ntdsutil and vssadmin as part of living-off-the-land tradecraft.

incident.analysis: Possession of NTDS.dit means every domain credential must be treated as compromised; recovery requires coordinated resets including KRBTGT.

indicators: Processes opening lsass.exe with read access (Sysmon 10)
ntdsutil 'ifm' or vssadmin create shadow on domain controllers
comsvcs.dll MiniDump usage
Copies of NTDS.dit or SYSTEM hive in temp paths
detections: Non-allow-listed process accessing LSASS memory
Shadow-copy creation followed by file copy from the shadow volume on a DC
Command lines containing 'ntds.dit' or 'ifm'
controls: Enable LSA protection (RunAsPPL) and Credential Guard
Limit domain admin logons to tier-0 systems
Monitor and restrict access to domain controllers
EDR with credential-theft prevention rules
response: Assume all credentials on the host (or the whole domain, for NTDS) are compromised
Reset privileged accounts and KRBTGT twice, with replication between resets
Hunt for use of dumped credentials
Rebuild compromised domain controllers if integrity is in doubt

references.title: AA24-038A: PRC State-Sponsored Actors Compromise and Maintain Persistent Access to U.S. Critical Infrastructure

attacks.name: Malware execution
attacks.overview: Getting malicious code to run on a host, commonly through a user opening a weaponised document that launches a script interpreter to download further payloads.
methodology: Deliver a malicious attachment or link
User enables content or opens the file
Macro or script launches an interpreter (PowerShell, wscript, rundll32)
Payload downloaded, persistence established, C2 contacted

incident.title: Emotet malicious-document campaigns

facts.text: CISA reported Emotet spreading primarily through phishing emails containing malicious attachments or links.
Emotet was used to drop other malware, including TrickBot and QakBot.

incident.analysis: Office-to-script-interpreter process chains remain one of the highest-value, lowest-noise detections for commodity malware.

indicators: winword.exe/excel.exe spawning powershell, cmd, wscript or rundll32
Encoded PowerShell command lines
Executables written to user temp or AppData directories
New Run keys or scheduled tasks
detections: Office parent process spawning a script interpreter
PowerShell with -enc / DownloadString / IEX
Persistence created within minutes of a document being opened
controls: Block macros from the internet (Mark-of-the-Web)
Attack Surface Reduction rules
Application control (WDAC/AppLocker)
PowerShell Constrained Language Mode and logging
response: Isolate the host and collect the document and dropped files
Identify other recipients of the same lure
Remove persistence and reimage if needed
Block C2 and download infrastructure

attacks.name: DNS tunnelling and DNS-based C2
attacks.overview: Encoding data or commands inside DNS queries and responses to communicate with attacker infrastructure, exploiting the fact that DNS is rarely blocked.
methodology: Register a domain with an attacker-controlled authoritative name server
Malware encodes data in subdomain labels (e.g. base32 chunks)
Responses (TXT, CNAME, A records) carry commands
Low-and-slow beaconing to blend with normal DNS

incident.title: SUNBURST backdoor DNS communications

facts.text: CISA reported that the SolarWinds Orion backdoor communicated with subdomains of avsvmcloud[.]com via DNS as part of its command-and-control.
FireEye (now Mandiant) described the backdoor encoding information in DNS subdomain requests before switching to HTTP for later stages.

incident.analysis: SUNBURST used DNS for beaconing and victim selection rather than bulk tunnelling, so volume-based detections alone would miss it; subdomain entropy and new-domain analytics are complementary.

indicators: Long, high-entropy subdomain labels
High volume of TXT or NULL queries to one domain
Many unique subdomains under a rarely seen parent domain
Hosts querying external resolvers directly
detections: Average label length or Shannon entropy above baseline per parent domain
Unique-subdomain count per domain per hour
Direct-to-internet DNS bypassing internal resolvers
controls: Force all DNS through monitored internal resolvers
Protective DNS / RPZ blocking of newly registered domains
Block outbound port 53 except from resolvers
Log and retain DNS queries
response: Sinkhole or block the domain
Identify all hosts that queried it
Recover encoded data where possible to assess exfiltration
Investigate the infected hosts for the implant

references.title: AA20-352A: Advanced Persistent Threat Compromise of Government Agencies, Critical Infrastructure, and Private Sector Organizations
Highly Evasive Attacker Leverages SolarWinds Supply Chain to Compromise Multiple Global Victims With SUNBURST Backdoor

attacks.name: Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS)
attacks.overview: Overwhelming a service's bandwidth, network devices or application resources with traffic from many sources so legitimate users cannot reach it.
methodology: Assemble attack capacity (botnets or reflection/amplification servers)
Choose a vector: volumetric (UDP amplification), protocol (SYN flood) or application layer (HTTP floods)
Launch, often in waves, sometimes alongside extortion demands

incident.title: GitHub memcached amplification attack

facts.text: GitHub reported an attack peaking at 1.35 Tbps that used memcached-based amplification.
GitHub was unavailable or intermittently available for about ten minutes before traffic was routed to its DDoS mitigation provider.

incident.analysis: Amplification vectors rely on misconfigured internet-exposed services; upstream scrubbing capacity, not on-premises appliances, is what absorbs terabit-scale floods.

indicators: Sudden traffic spikes from many sources
Large volumes of UDP responses from port 11211, 123, 53 or 1900
Exhausted connection tables and rising latency
Extortion emails threatening attacks
detections: Traffic volume beyond baseline thresholds per destination
Protocol mix anomalies (e.g., spike in UDP fragments)
Application request-rate anomalies per client
controls: Upstream DDoS protection / scrubbing service
CDN and anycast distribution
Rate limiting and autoscaling
Don't expose amplification-prone services (memcached, open resolvers)
Documented DDoS runbook with your ISP
response: Activate the mitigation provider and ISP escalation path
Apply filters for the identified vector
Communicate status to users
Review post-incident and adjust thresholds

references.title: Understanding and Responding to Distributed Denial-of-Service Attacks

attacks.name: Supply-chain attacks
attacks.overview: Compromising a trusted supplier, its software build or its update channel so that malicious code reaches many downstream organisations through legitimate distribution.
methodology: Compromise a vendor's development or build environment
Insert malicious code into a signed release or update
Customers install the trusted update
Selectively activate against high-value victims

incident.title: 3CXDesktopApp supply-chain compromise

facts.text: CISA reported a supply-chain attack affecting 3CXDesktopApp, in which trojanised versions of the legitimate, signed desktop application were distributed.
CISA urged users to review the vendor's guidance and to hunt for related malicious activity.

incident.analysis: Code signing proves origin, not integrity of the build process; behavioural monitoring of trusted applications is necessary because allow-lists will trust them.

indicators: Trusted applications making connections to newly observed domains
Unexpected child processes from signed vendor software
Vendor security advisories or EDR detections for widely deployed software
detections: New outbound destinations for long-installed software
Signed binary loading unsigned or newly modified DLLs
Retro-hunt historical logs when an IOC set is published
controls: Software inventory and SBOMs
Vendor risk management and secure-development requirements
Network egress restrictions for servers and apps
Staged rollout of updates where possible
response: Identify all installations and versions
Isolate or uninstall affected versions per vendor guidance
Hunt for follow-on activity on affected hosts
Rotate credentials accessible to the compromised software

attacks.name: Exploitation of known vulnerabilities
attacks.overview: Exploiting publicly disclosed vulnerabilities for which patches exist but have not been applied, especially on internet-facing systems.
methodology: Scan the internet for vulnerable versions shortly after disclosure
Use public or commodity exploits
Gain code execution and deploy web shells or tools
Pivot internally and exfiltrate

incident.title: Equifax breach via unpatched Apache Struts

facts.text: Attackers exploited a known vulnerability in the Apache Struts web framework (CVE-2017-5638) in an Equifax online dispute portal that had not been patched.
According to the GAO, the attackers accessed personal information of at least 145.5 million individuals.

incident.analysis: The patch was available before the intrusion began; asset inventory and patch verification failures, not lack of a fix, enabled the breach.

indicators: Exploit-pattern requests in web logs shortly after a CVE disclosure
Web server processes spawning shells
New files in web roots
Vulnerability scanner showing unpatched KEV-listed CVEs
detections: Web server process (w3wp, httpd, java) spawning cmd, sh or PowerShell
IDS signatures for newly published exploits
Correlate scanner findings with internet exposure
controls: Prioritise patching using CISA KEV and EPSS
Maintain an accurate internet-facing asset inventory
Virtual patching via WAF as an interim measure
Verify patches were actually applied (rescan)
response: Patch or isolate the vulnerable system immediately
Hunt for web shells and persistence
Scope data access via logs
Review why the patch was missed and fix the process

references.title: Data Protection: Actions Taken by Equifax and Federal Agencies in Response to the 2017 Breach (GAO-18-559)
